'''Matthew O'Brien''' (1814–1855) was an Irish [[mathematician]].

== Life and work ==
O'Brien was born at [[Ennis]] ([[county Clare]]) son of a medical doctor.<ref>{{smallcaps|Lynch}}, page 81.</ref> In 1830 he was admitted in the [[Trinity College, Dublin]], and in 1834 in the [[Caius College]] ([[university of Cambridge]]) where he graduated in 1838 as third ''wrangler'',<ref>{{smallcaps|Crowe}}, page 97.</ref> as pupil of [[William Hopkins]].<ref>{{smallcaps|Lynch}}, page 82.</ref> During a brief period (1840–1841) he was fellow of Caius College.<ref>{{smallcaps|Craik}}, page 169.</ref>

From 1844 to 1854 he was lecturer on Natural Philosophy and Mathematics at [[King's College London]], he simultaneously held the post of lecturer on Astronomy in the [[Royal Military Academy, Woolwich]].<ref>{{smallcaps|Craik}}, page 219.</ref>

O'Brien was the author of twenty mathematical papers and some elementary textbooks. His most notable contribution was in theory and application of the vector method,<ref>{{smallcaps|Lynch}}, page 83.</ref> in a set of papers published between 1846 and 1852.<ref>{{smallcaps|Smith}}, page 174.</ref> However, he did not finish fully developing the method because some of his theories were unsatisfactory,<ref>{{smallcaps|Craik}}, page 335.</ref> and because he failed to include a treatment of associativity.<ref>{{smallcaps|Crowe}}, page 100.</ref> His work was very innovative, but his ideas were almost completely ignored by his contemporaries.<ref>{{smallcaps|Lynch}}, page 86.</ref>
